UNTP — the UN Transparency Protocol — is targeting a 1.0 Digital Product Passport specification release on 1 September 2026, built on the same W3C Verifiable Credentials Data Model 2.0 this protocol’s records already use.

Why AuthiChain

  • UNTP issues every credential, including its Digital Product Passport, as a W3C VC 2.0 object — the identical base data model documented in SPEC.md §2, not a competing format
  • UNTP is UN/CEFACT and UNECE work, currently on 0.6.x pilot releases; SPEC.md is a v0.1.0 draft — both are pre-1.0 specs published for implementers to compare, not finished standards
  • The 28-fixture conformance suite and reference verifier are public, so the gap between a ProvenanceRecord and a UNTP DigitalProductPassport credential is something an implementer can check directly, not take on faith

How it works

Issue a unique identifier per unit, anchor its record on-chain for tamper-evidence, and let anyone verify it with a single scan. Plans start at $49/mo.

FAQ

Is a record issued under this protocol a valid UNTP DigitalProductPassport credential?

Not directly — UNTP defines its own credential type and JSON-LD context on top of VC 2.0. This protocol’s ProvenanceRecord shares the base standard but is a different schema; mapping between them is inspectable, not assumed.

When does UNTP 1.0 ship?

The UNTP team is targeting a 1.0 release on 1 September 2026; current releases are versioned 0.6.x and marked suitable for pilot implementations.

title: Digital Product Passport Access Rights | AuthiChain
metaDescription: ESPR splits Digital Product Passport access into tiers — public, professional/economic-operator, and authority — and the registry rule this protocol already.
bodyHtml:
ESPR splits Digital Product Passport access into tiers — public, professional/economic-operator, and authority — and the registry rule this protocol already implements, a permanent URL with no authentication, is exactly what the public tier requires.

Why AuthiChain

  • Annex XIII and the Article 77(9) implementing act govern which fields each tier sees; the split is defined per product-group delegated act, not by this protocol
  • SPEC.md §6 requires records to resolve from a permanent URL without authentication — verification that requires an account is not public verification, and that is the public tier by definition
  • Field-level restriction for confidential technical data is not in spec v0.1.0 — every field in a record issued today is visible to anyone who resolves its URL, which is the public-tier behavior and not yet the professional or authority tiers

How it works

Issue a unique identifier per unit, anchor its record on-chain for tamper-evidence, and let anyone verify it with a single scan. Plans start at $49/mo.

FAQ

Does this protocol already support ESPR-style tiered access?

Not yet — v0.1.0 issues one record with one visibility level. Tiering confidential fields for repairers, recyclers, or authorities is a real requirement the delegated acts will define, and it is not built here.

Is a single public record still useful before tiering exists?

Yes, for the tier ESPR requires to be free and unauthenticated — which is how every record resolves today.

h1: QR Code Phishing Product Packaging Security
bodyHtml:
Quishing — QR codes cloned or altered to redirect a scan to a fake destination — is a documented, rising attack pattern in 2026, and a plain QR code has no way to prove what it points to is genuine; a signed AuthiChain record does.

Why AuthiChain

  • Verification checks an Ed25519 signature against the record itself, not just that a URL resolves — a cloned code pointing to fabricated content fails the check
  • Offline verification means a scanner is not just trusting whichever server happens to answer at scan time
  • A signature proves who issued the record, not that the physical item in hand matches it — stated plainly in protocol/SPEC.md §8

How it works

Issue a unique identifier per unit, anchor its record on-chain for tamper-evidence, and let anyone verify it with a single scan. Plans start at $49/mo.

FAQ

Can a counterfeit copy an AuthiChain QR code and still pass?

The printed code can be copied, but reproducing a valid Ed25519 signature over fabricated content cannot — a cloned code pointing anywhere but the genuine record fails signature verification.

Does this protect against quishing generally?

It stops a cloned code from passing as a genuine AuthiChain record. It does not secure QR codes outside this protocol — any code that is not signed is a separate risk a scanner has to judge on its own.

title: DID Key Vs DID Web For Verifiable Credentials | AuthiChain
metaDescription: A Verifiable Credential’s issuer identifier has to resolve to a public key somehow — did:key embeds the key directly in the identifier so no network lookup.
h1: DID Key Vs DID Web For Verifiable Credentials
bodyHtml:
A Verifiable Credential’s issuer identifier has to resolve to a public key somehow — did:key embeds the key directly in the identifier so no network lookup is needed, while did:web ties resolution to a domain you control, which is why AuthiChain’s protocol spec uses did:key by default.

Why AuthiChain

  • did:key needs no DNS, hosting, or network call to resolve — the public key is the identifier, which is what makes offline verification possible at all
  • did:web ties portability to a domain: lose the domain and every credential issued under that method stops resolving
  • protocol/SPEC.md §5 step 2 resolves the issuer key from did:key with zero network access, matching the spec’s offline-verification requirement

How it works

Issue a unique identifier per unit, anchor its record on-chain for tamper-evidence, and let anyone verify it with a single scan. Plans start at $49/mo.

FAQ

Why not use did:web since we already control a domain?

You can — the spec does not forbid it. But did:web makes verification depend on your DNS and hosting staying reachable, which works against the goal of a verifier reaching a verdict without contacting anyone.

Does did:key support key rotation?

Not on its own — a new key is a new identifier. That gap is part of what credentialStatus and revocation, planned for v0.2, are meant to address.

title: C2pa Content Credentials Vs Product Provenance | AuthiChain
metaDescription: C2PA Content Credentials reached version 2.3 in January 2026 and answer a question about a file — who captured this image, what edited it, was AI involved —.
h1: C2pa Content Credentials Vs Product Provenance
bodyHtml:
C2PA Content Credentials reached version 2.3 in January 2026 and answer a question about a file — who captured this image, what edited it, was AI involved — while a product provenance record answers a question about a physical object, which is why the two are complements rather than alternatives.

Why AuthiChain

  • C2PA binds a manifest to the bytes of a media file; a provenance record binds a signature to an item identifier that has no bytes to hash, so the binding to the physical object comes from the printed carrier, not from cryptography
  • Both are tamper-evident in the same way: alter the signed content and the signature stops matching — the difference is what the signature is over, not how strong it is
  • Neither proves the claim inside is true. C2PA proves a camera or tool signed a file; an Ed25519 provenance signature proves an issuer signed a statement — protocol/SPEC.md §8 states plainly that signatures prove authorship, not truth

How it works

Issue a unique identifier per unit, anchor its record on-chain for tamper-evidence, and let anyone verify it with a single scan. Plans start at $49/mo.

FAQ

Can C2PA authenticate a physical product?

Not on its own. C2PA is a media-provenance specification: its manifest is bound to a file’s bytes. A photograph of a product can carry Content Credentials proving how the photo was made, but that says nothing about whether the object in it is genuine.

Would C2PA and a product provenance record be used together?

They can be. Product images and certificates attached to a passport are files, and C2PA can establish how those files were produced, while the signed provenance record establishes who issued the claim about the item itself.

metaDescription: NIST finalized three post-quantum signature standards — ML-DSA (FIPS 204), SLH-DSA (FIPS 205), and the key-encapsulation ML-KEM (FIPS 203) — and AuthiChain’s.
bodyHtml:
NIST finalized three post-quantum signature standards — ML-DSA (FIPS 204), SLH-DSA (FIPS 205), and the key-encapsulation ML-KEM (FIPS 203) — and AuthiChain’s protocol spec states plainly, in SPEC.md §8, that its current Ed25519 suite is not one of them.

  • Ed25519 (RFC 8032) is what protocol/SPEC.md specifies today — fast, small signatures, and explicitly not post-quantum secure, the same kind of direct disclosure Section 8 makes about revocation
  • Records signed now and read years from now carry Store-Now-Decrypt-Later exposure if an adversary archives them for a future quantum break — a risk shared by any long-lived credential, not unique to this protocol
  • The record’s proof.type field names the signature suite per record, so a future ML-DSA or SLH-DSA suite is a new proof type, not a rewrite of every record already issued

Issue a unique identifier per unit, anchor its record on-chain for tamper-evidence, and let anyone verify it with a single scan. Plans start at $49/mo.

FAQ

Is Ed25519 quantum-resistant?

No. Ed25519 is elliptic-curve cryptography under FIPS 186-5 / RFC 8032 and falls to Shor’s algorithm on a sufficiently large quantum computer — the same limit stated in protocol/SPEC.md §8.

Does AuthiChain support ML-DSA or SLH-DSA today?

No — the reference verifier implements Ed25519 only. NIST published FIPS 204 and FIPS 205 as post-quantum signature standards; adopting one is a spec extension the protocol has not shipped.

  • protocol/SPEC.md §3.2 requires RFC 8785 (JCS) canonicalization specifically so two independent verifiers derive byte-identical input from the same record — a property any of the three securing mechanisms could satisfy, but only Data Integrity is what is actually implemented today

How it works

Is a Data Integrity proof less standard than SD-JWT?

No — both are W3C-defined ways to secure the same VC Data Model 2.0 credential. VC-JOSE-COSE and Data Integrity are parallel securing mechanisms, not a newer one replacing an older one.

Not today — the reference verifier implements Ed25519 Data Integrity proofs only. Selective disclosure matters more for identity credentials than for a provenance record meant to be checked in full.

h1: Verified By GS1 Vs Blockchain Provenance Record
bodyHtml:
Verified by GS1 checks whether a GTIN, GLN, or company identifier is real and who registered it, against data the brand owner submitted to GS1’s own registry — a different question from whether one specific physical unit’s record is signed and unaltered, which is what a QRON scan checks.

Why QRON

  • Verified by GS1 answers “does this identifier exist and who owns it” at the registry level — it doesn’t check a per-unit signature, so two items sharing one genuine GTIN pass a Verified by GS1 lookup identically, counterfeit or not
  • A QRON record ties an Ed25519 signature to one serialized item’s data, not to the identifier class it belongs to — a distinction GS1 Digital Link Sunrise 2027’s move to 2D barcodes does not by itself resolve
  • The two aren’t competitors: one GS1 Digital Link URL can resolve to both a Verified by GS1-style identity lookup and a signed provenance record, selected by linkType, from the same printed code

Issue a unique identifier per unit, anchor its record on-chain for tamper-evidence, and let anyone verify it with a single scan. Plans start at $29/mo.

FAQ

Does Verified by GS1 stop counterfeiting?

It confirms an identifier and its registered owner are genuine, which catches a fabricated or unassigned GTIN. It doesn’t verify that a specific physical unit carrying a real GTIN is the genuine item — a counterfeit using a real product’s GTIN on a fake unit still passes a Verified by GS1 check.

Do we need both Verified by GS1 and a signed provenance record?

They answer different questions. Verified by GS1 is useful for confirming a partner’s identifier is legitimately registered before you list a product; a signed per-unit record is what proves the specific item a customer is holding is genuine.

title: EBSI Trust Registry Vs DID Key | AuthiChain
metaDescription: EBSI, the EU’s own blockchain infrastructure for verifiable credentials, resolves trust through a governed Trusted Issuers Registry — a verifier checks.
h1: EBSI Trust Registry Vs DID Key
bodyHtml:
EBSI, the EU’s own blockchain infrastructure for verifiable credentials, resolves trust through a governed Trusted Issuers Registry — a verifier checks whether an issuer’s DID is accredited on that list before trusting a credential, the opposite model from the did:key default protocol/SPEC.md §5 uses, where the key itself is the entire trust anchor.

Why AuthiChain

  • A Trusted Issuers Registry answers “is this issuer accredited to issue this schema” — a governance question a registry operator controls; did:key answers only “did this specific keypair sign this record,” with no accreditation layer at all
  • EBSI’s model fits a use case where who is allowed to issue matters, like diplomas or professional credentials; a physical-item provenance record cares which specific issuer signed it, not whether a central registry pre-approved them — why protocol/SPEC.md keeps verification independent of any registry lookup
  • A registry-based trust model requires the registry to stay reachable for a verifier to check accreditation; did:key resolves the issuer key with zero network access, matching this protocol’s offline-verification requirement — a tradeoff, not a strictly better or worse choice

How it works

Issue a unique identifier per unit, anchor its record on-chain for tamper-evidence, and let anyone verify it with a single scan. Plans start at $49/mo.

FAQ

Does AuthiChain use EBSI or a trust registry?

No — the reference verifier resolves did:key directly, per protocol/SPEC.md §5, with no registry lookup. A verifier checks the signature against the key embedded in the identifier itself.

Would a trust-registry model work for product provenance records?

It could, at the cost of the offline-verification property this protocol optimizes for: a registry check means a verifier depends on that registry being reachable, which did:key’s self-contained resolution avoids by design.

title: Battery Passport Second Life Repurposing | AuthiChain
metaDescription: When an EV battery is pulled for second-life use in stationary storage, EU rules treat the repurposed unit as a new product — the operator repurposing it has.
bodyHtml:
When an EV battery is pulled for second-life use in stationary storage, EU rules treat the repurposed unit as a new product — the operator repurposing it has to issue a new battery passport with a new QR code that references the original battery’s history, not just relabel the old passport.

Why AuthiChain

  • A new passport for a repurposed battery is a new signed record with its own identifier — the same one-record-per-physical-unit model this protocol already uses, not a mutation of the original battery’s record
  • The new record has to reference the original battery’s passport, so a second-life buyer traces composition, usage history, and state-of-health back through both records instead of trusting a fresh passport with no lineage
  • The 18 February 2027 mandate applies to any battery over 2 kWh placed on the market from that date, including a repurposed one — a second-life operator entering the market after that date is a covered economic operator, not an exception to it

How it works

Issue a unique identifier per unit, anchor its record on-chain for tamper-evidence, and let anyone verify it with a single scan. Plans start at $49/mo.

FAQ

Can a second-life battery keep its original passport?

No — repurposing or remanufacturing a battery for a new use makes it a new product under EU rules. The repurposing operator issues a new passport and QR code, referencing the original battery’s history rather than replacing it.

Who is responsible for issuing the second-life passport?

The economic operator that repurposes or remanufactures the battery — not the original manufacturer — becomes responsible for the new passport once the battery re-enters the market as a distinct product.
